2025_331_8_c_bond_resolution_sbqlp_troy_.paragraph: Bond authorizing resolution presented to the Board of Education of the Troy School District, County of Oakland, Michigan, at its regular meeting of November 18, 2025, covering the 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation). It authorizes an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $220,000,000, of which not more than $193,000,000 is the second series under the $555,000,000 proposal approved by voters on November 8, 2022; the balance would currently refund the 2016 School Building and Site Bonds maturing May 1, 2027 through May 1, 2032. Sale is negotiated, with Huntington Securities, Inc. as senior managing underwriter.
2025_331_8_c_bond_resolution_sbqlp_troy_.page:
**Item:** 8.C. Bond Resolution (SBQLP) - Troy 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds, document 44944687.1, before the Board of Education of the Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, at a regular meeting held in the School District on November 18, 2025 at 7:00 p.m. local time. The certification page carries the signature block of Emina Alic, Secretary, Board of Education, with an Open Meetings Act (Act 267, Public Acts of 1976) compliance certificate. The adoption blanks for PRESENT, ABSENT, the offering and supporting members, and the AYES/NAYS tallies are unfilled in this draft.

**Authorization background**

- At the General School Election of November 8, 2022, electors approved bonds in one or more series not to exceed $555,000,000 for remodeling and re-equipping school buildings, athletic fields and playgrounds; erecting a replacement middle school and classroom additions; instructional technology infrastructure; site acquisition and improvement; and the purchase of school buses.
- Tax levies are without limitation as to rate or amount under Article IX, Sections 6 and 16 of the Michigan Constitution of 1963.
- The first series, the 2023 School Building and Site Bonds dated March 7, 2023, was issued in the original principal amount of $171,370,000 with net original issue premium of $18,629,212.85, which counts against the $555,000,000 authorization.
- The Prior Bonds proposed for refunding are the 2016 School Building and Site Bonds dated December 28, 2016; the Refunded Bonds are those maturing May 1, 2027 through May 1, 2032, inclusive.

**Sale parameters**

| Parameter | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| Aggregate principal amount | not to exceed $220,000,000 |
| New money (Projects) portion | not to exceed $193,000,000 |
| True interest cost | not to exceed 5.50% per annum |
| Underwriter's discount | not to exceed 0.75% of principal |
| Net present value refunding savings threshold | at least 3.00% |
| Final maturity | not later than 30 years from date of issue |
| Denomination | $5,000 or integral multiples |

If the Authorized Officer, on the Municipal Advisor's advice, determines the net present value savings on the refunding falls below 3.00%, the district may instead issue up to $193,000,000 of new money only, redesignated 2026 School Building and Site Bonds.

**Professionals and structure**

- Underwriter: Huntington Securities, Inc., senior managing underwriter, with authority to appoint co-managers.
- Bond Counsel: Miller, Canfield, Paddock and Stone, P.L.C., approved notwithstanding its periodic unrelated representation of Huntington Securities, Inc.
- Municipal Advisor: PFM Financial Advisors LLC.
- Authorized Officer: the Superintendent and the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, either acting individually.
- Bonds mature May 1 and/or November 1, with semi-annual interest; book-entry-only through The Depository Trust Company, New York, New York; registered owner in Exhibit A is Cede & Co.

**Funds created:** 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds Debt Retirement Fund, Capital Projects Fund, Cost of Issuance Fund, and an Escrow Fund held by an Escrow Agent under an Escrow Agreement to pay the Refunded Bonds.

**Other provisions:** unlimited tax levy duty commencing with the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2026; Treasury qualification under the School Bond Qualification, Approval, and Loan Act, Act 92, Public Acts of Michigan, 2005; reimbursement declarations under Treas. Reg. Section 1.150-2 with maximum debt for the Projects stated as $193,000,000; and a continuing disclosure undertaking under SEC Rule 15c2-12 with first filing for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2026.
2025_331_8_c_bond_resolution_sbqlp_troy_.verbose:
Resolution of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, authorizing the 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), presented as agenda item 8.C. and identified as document 44944687.1. It is offered at a regular meeting held in the School District on November 18, 2025, at 7:00 p.m., local time; the lines for PRESENT and ABSENT members, for the offering and supporting members, and for the AYES and NAYS tallies remain blank in the version presented. The closing certification, signed by Emina Alic, Secretary, Board of Education, attests that the copy is true and complete and that notice was given in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of 1976, as amended.

RECITALS. At the General School Election held in the School District on November 8, 2022, qualified electors approved the issuance of bonds, in one or more series, in an amount not to exceed $555,000,000 (the 2022 Bond Proposal), for remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings, athletic fields and playgrounds; erecting, equipping and furnishing a replacement middle school and classroom additions; acquiring and installing instructional technology infrastructure and equipment; acquiring and improving sites; and the purchase of school buses (the Projects). Under Section 6, Article IX and Section 16, Article IX of the Michigan Constitution of 1963, the tax levies for those bonds are without limitation as to rate or amount. The School District previously issued its 2023 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), dated March 7, 2023, in the original principal amount of $171,370,000 as the first series under the 2022 Bond Proposal; because of prevailing market conditions those bonds were issued with net original issue premium of $18,629,212.85, which counts against the $555,000,000 authorization. The Board now desires to authorize a second series in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $193,000,000 to pay Project costs and a portion of issuance costs. Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended, permits refunding of funded indebtedness; the School District previously issued its 2016 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), dated December 28, 2016 (the Prior Bonds), and the Board determines it is in the district's best interest to currently refund all or a portion of the Prior Bonds maturing May 1, 2027 through May 1, 2032, inclusive (the Refunded Bonds). Because the source of payment is the same and to reduce issuance and administration cost, the Board combines the new money and refunding issues into a single series in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $220,000,000 while maintaining a separate capital projects fund for the Projects. If market interest rates rise so that the refunding becomes noneconomic or inefficient, the Board retains the option of authorizing only the $193,000,000 new money issue.

ISSUANCE AND PARAMETERS. The Bonds may be issued in one or more series in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $220,000,000, or such lesser amount as the Authorized Officer determines upon sale, to finance a portion of the Projects, refund the Refunded Bonds, and pay costs of issuance. The Projects portion shall not exceed $193,000,000. If the Authorized Officer, on the advice of the Municipal Advisor, determines that net present value savings from the refinancing are not at least 3.00% of the principal of the Refunded Bonds, the district may issue Bonds of not more than $193,000,000 for the Projects and associated issuance costs only, in which case the Bonds are redesignated 2026 School Building and Site Bonds.

BOND DETAILS. Bonds are registered as to principal and interest in denominations of $5,000 or integral multiples, dated as of the date of delivery or another date set by the Authorized Officer, and numbered as determined by the Transfer Agent. Maturities fall on May 1 and/or November 1 in years and amounts fixed at sale, with final maturity not later than thirty (30) years from the date of issue. Interest is set at negotiated sale at a rate or rates not exceeding a true interest cost of 5.50% per annum, payable semi-annually on May 1 and November 1. The underwriter's discount shall not exceed 0.75% of principal. Interest is payable by check mailed to the registered owner of record as of the fifteenth day of the month preceding each payment date. The Bonds may be issued in book-entry-only form through The Depository Trust Company in New York, New York, and may be serial or term bonds subject to optional or mandatory redemption. Bonds are signed by manual or facsimile signatures of the President and Secretary of the Board and are not valid until authenticated by the Transfer Agent.

FUNDS. Unless a Common Debt Retirement Fund is established, the Treasurer opens a special depositary account designated the 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds Debt Retirement Fund, into which all tax proceeds levied for principal, interest and redemption price are deposited, together with any accrued interest received on delivery. A special depository account designated the 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds Projects Fund (the Capital Projects Fund) receives the amounts specified at sale from net proceeds and net original issue premium, to be used solely for Project costs and, as needed, to rebate arbitrage earnings to the United States Department of Treasury under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended. Costs of issuance are deposited into a separate 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds Cost of Issuance Fund; residual balances there are allocated between the Capital Projects Fund and the Debt Retirement Fund on the advice of Bond Counsel. Money remaining in the Capital Projects Fund after completion may be used first for any purpose permitted by the 2022 Bond Proposal and second for any other lawful purpose; net original issue premium attributable to the new money portion counts against the 2022 Bond Proposal authorization. The Escrow Fund holds the balance of proceeds plus moneys transferred from the Prior Bonds debt retirement funds, invested in obligations of or guaranteed by the United States of America sufficient without reinvestment to pay the Refunded Bonds; the Escrow Agent acts under an Escrow Agreement irrevocably directing the call for redemption of the specified Prior Bonds.

TAX LEVY, SALE METHOD AND PROFESSIONALS. Commencing with the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2026, the School District must levy annually a tax sufficient to pay principal and interest as due, without limitation as to rate or amount. Having compared competitive and negotiated sale under Act 34 and on the Municipal Advisor's advice, the Board determines that a negotiated sale provides greater flexibility in structuring maturities and timing. Huntington Securities, Inc. is appointed senior managing underwriter, with the Authorized Officer permitted to appoint co-managing underwriters if the Municipal Advisor recommends. The Authorized Officer, defined as the Superintendent and the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, either acting individually, may negotiate, award, execute and deliver the bond purchase agreement without further Board approval provided the true interest cost does not exceed 5.50% per annum, net present value savings are not less than 3.00% of projected debt service on the Refunded Bonds under Treasury guidelines, and the underwriter's discount does not exceed 0.75% of principal. The Authorized Officer may execute a sale order evidencing final terms, apply for bond ratings, and purchase municipal bond insurance if deemed appropriate. Miller, Canfield, Paddock and Stone, P.L.C. is appointed Bond Counsel, approved notwithstanding Miller Canfield's periodic representation in unrelated matters of Huntington Securities, Inc. PFM Financial Advisors LLC is appointed financial advisor (Municipal Advisor). The Authorized Officer may apply to the Michigan Department of Treasury for prior approval or file a qualifying statement, request waivers including rating waivers, file a Security Report under Act 34, and seek qualification under the School Bond Qualification, Approval, and Loan Act, Act 92, Public Acts of Michigan, 2005, as amended; the Secretary of the Board is directed to submit the completed Application for Final Qualification.

TAX AND REIMBURSEMENT MATTERS. The district covenants to maintain the exclusion of interest from adjusted gross income for federal income tax purposes under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. Reimbursement declarations under Treas. Reg. Section 1.150-2 state that the district expects to reimburse itself from bond proceeds for Project expenditures paid subsequent to sixty (60) days prior to the resolution date; that the maximum principal amount of debt expected for the Projects, including issuance costs, is $193,000,000; and that reimbursement allocation will occur not later than 18 months after the later of payment or placed-in-service, and in no event more than three (3) years after the original expenditure. All conflicting resolutions and parts of resolutions are rescinded.

EXHIBITS. Exhibit A is the bond form, showing Registered Owner Cede & Co., interest computed on a 360-day year of twelve 30-day months, issuance under Act 451, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976, as amended, and Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended, pursuant to the resolution adopted November 18, 2025 as the second series authorized by the November 8, 2022 election; redemption notice at least 30 days and not more than 60 days before the redemption date; calls in multiples of $5,000; full faith and credit irrevocably pledged; Certificate of Authentication dated 2026. Exhibit B is the form of Continuing Disclosure Undertaking under SEC Rule 15c2-12, requiring filing with the MSRB through EMMA on or before the last day of the sixth month after fiscal year end, commencing with the fiscal year ending June 30, 2026, of Audited Financial Statements and tables covering Historical Enrollment, State Aid Payments, Property Valuations, Major Taxpayers, School District Tax Rates per $1,000 of valuation, Tax Levies and Collections, Contribution to MPSERS, Debt Statement Direct Debt, the School Loan Revolving Fund (SLRF) Program, and the current-year General Fund Budget Summary in Appendix C; it also lists material event notices due within ten business days, including payment delinquencies, defeasances, rating changes, bankruptcy, and incurrence of a Financial Obligation. Exhibit C is the form of Application for Final Qualification of Bonds.

2025_332_september_2025_financial_statem.paragraph: Monthly financial report to the Troy School District Board of Education for the November 18, 2025 meeting, presenting unaudited Statements of Revenues and Expenditures for the period July 1, 2025 through September 30, 2025 across nine funds. 2025_332_september_2025_financial_statem.verbose:
Troy School District monthly financial statement package for the Board of Education meeting of November 18, 2025, covering the period July 1, 2025 through September 30, 2025 (unaudited). Nine separate Statements of Revenues and Expenditures are presented, each with an Approved Budget column and an Actual column.

GENERAL FUND. Revenues: Local Sources budget 47,484,756, actual 22,864,002; State Sources budget 123,879,792, actual 15,452,721; Federal Sources budget 4,617,113, no actual recorded; Interdistrict Sources no budget, actual 2,938,611; Transfers In and Other budget 14,564,324, no actual recorded. Total Revenues budget 190,545,983, actual 41,255,335. Expenditures, Instruction: Basic Programs budget 91,715,371, actual 17,499,215; Added Needs budget 30,930,228, actual 6,228,003; Adult Education budget 969,620, actual 54,716; Total Instruction budget 123,615,219, actual 23,781,934. Support Services: Pupil budget 15,850,349, actual 3,090,072; Instructional Staff budget 10,854,009, actual 2,802,230; General Administration budget 2,321,066, actual 668,737; School Administration budget 10,316,176, actual 2,715,450; Business Services budget 1,771,358, actual 517,319; Operations budget 15,811,567, actual 4,694,646; Pupil Transportation budget 6,244,591, actual 475,478; Central Services budget 3,723,546, actual 1,286,872; Support Services (Athletics and Other) budget 2,927,106, actual 1,087,982; Total Support Services budget 69,819,768, actual 17,338,785. Total Expenditures budget 2,490,615, actual 542,458. Revenues Over (Under) Expenditures: budget (218,518), actual 108,400.

SPECIAL REVENUE FUND - TROY CAREER CENTER FUND (529). Revenues: State Sources budget 598,948, actual 142,178; Federal Sources budget 2,745,238, actual 320,522. Total Revenues budget 3,344,186, actual 462,701. Total Expenditures budget 3,344,186, actual 879,683. Revenues Over (Under) Expenditures: budget 0, actual (416,982). Capital Outlay is the category where actual spending has already passed the annual budget figure, and federal reimbursement revenue lags the spending it supports.

SPECIAL REVENUE FUND - FOOD SERVICE FUND (520). Revenues: Local Sources budget 323,838, actual 30,612; State Sources budget 6,101,199, actual 37,785; Federal Sources budget 2,231,477, actual 457,800; Interdistrict Sources budget 718, no actual. Total Revenues budget 8,657,232, actual 526,198. Expenditures: Salaries budget 99,368, actual 29,524; Employee Benefits budget 7,602, actual 3,287; Purchased Services budget 3,724,193, actual 723,006; Supplies and Materials budget 4,552,315, actual 628,803; Capital Outlay budget 1,386,680, actual 379,014; Other budget 22,800, actual 7,598; Transfers Out budget 42,000, no actual. Total Expenditures budget 9,834,958, actual 1,771,231. Revenues Over (Under) Expenditures: budget (1,177,726), actual (1,245,034). State meal reimbursement revenue is the largest budgeted line for this fund but had barely begun to post by September 30, while purchased services and food supplies were already flowing, producing the negative actual position.

SINKING FUND (498). Revenues: Local Sources budget 5,225,572, actual 2,590,502; Total Revenue budget 5,225,572, actual 2,590,502. Expenditures: Supplies and Materials none budgeted, actual 618; Capital Outlay budget 2,125,000, actual 1,085,378. Total Expenditures budget 2,125,000, actual 1,085,997. Revenues Over (Under) Expenditures: budget 3,100,572, actual 1,504,505. The sinking fund is one of only two funds showing a positive budgeted bottom line for the year.

2023 CAPITAL PROJECTS FUND (423). Revenues: Local Sources budget 3,996,374, no actual recorded; Total Revenue budget 3,996,374, actual none. Expenditures: Purchased Services budget 905,393, actual 225,930; Capital Outlay budget 65,180,650, actual 11,595,950; Outgoing Transfers budget 977,864, actual 30,701. Total Expenditures budget 67,063,907, actual 11,852,580. Revenues Over (Under) Expenditures: budget (63,067,533), actual (11,852,580). This is by far the largest spending fund in the package, drawing down 2023 bond proceeds for the district's building program; because proceeds were received in a prior period, current-period revenue is nil and the entire actual expenditure figure flows through as a deficit for the quarter.

2019 CAPITAL PROJECTS FUND (419). Revenues: Local Sources budget 30,000, no actual; Total Revenue budget 30,000, actual none. Expenditures: Capital Outlay budget 1,034,912, no actual; Support Services - Central, none budgeted and none actual. Total Expenditures budget 1,034,912, no actual. Revenues Over (Under) Expenditures: budget (1,004,912), actual none. The 2019 fund recorded no transactions during the first quarter of the fiscal year.

OVERALL. Across the package, the General Fund and the sinking fund ended the quarter with revenues exceeding expenditures on an actual basis, as did the consolidated debt service funds, the Troy Preschool Fund and the Community Service Fund. The Troy Career Center Fund, the Food Service Fund and the 2023 Capital Projects Fund each recorded actual expenditures in excess of actual revenues. All figures are unaudited and cover only the first three months of the fiscal year that began July 1, 2025.

2025_333_2026_01_09_ocsba_resolutions_wi.paragraph: Packet of Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) resolutions distributed for the December 9, 2025 Troy School District Board meeting in advance of the January 9, 2026 OCSBA resolution vote, containing two proposed new resolutions plus the association's continuing resolutions. Under OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5, a resolution approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts becomes the official position of the association. The two new proposals would put OCSBA on record supporting non-partisan school board elections, in response to House Bill 4588, and full funding of Early On Michigan, the state's Part C early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three.
2025_333_2026_01_09_ocsba_resolutions_wi.page:
**Board meeting:** Troy School District, December 9, 2025.

**Document:** Five-page OCSBA resolutions packet headed "Proposed New Resolutions for January 2026" / "Proposed Amendments for January 2026." OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5 states that resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts shall be the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors.

**Proposed new resolution #1 - Non-partisan school board elections**

OCSBA supports non-partisan school board elections. The rationale responds to HB 4588, then moving through the state House (legislature.mi.gov, ObjectName 2025-HB-4588). Partisan elections are argued to decrease the number of willing candidates; increase campaign costs, since members would have to win both a primary and the November election; align local education decisions with party interests rather than student needs; and exclude thousands of current or potential board members, including federal employees legally prohibited from running in partisan races.

**Proposed new resolution #2 - Early On Michigan**

OCSBA supports full funding of Early On Michigan, an early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays, or at risk for delays due to certain health conditions. The rationale notes that the Michigan Mandatory Special Education law (MMSE) requires services for eligible children from birth through age 25; IDEA Part B covers ages 3 through 21 and IDEA Part C covers birth through age 2, which Michigan calls Early On; services for ages 22 through 25 fall under MMSE. Early On is coordinated by the Michigan Department of Education, funded to communities through their local Intermediate School District, and guided locally by an interagency coordinating council and memoranda of understanding among education, mental health, public health and social services.

| Early On funding | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Estimated annual cost of high-quality services | $230M |
| Recommended state appropriation (60% of estimated cost) | at least $138M |
| Section 54d, FY26 School Aid Act state funding | $48M |

The rationale also notes 50 years of advocacy for IDEA funding and the congressional promise to fund 40% of the cost of special education, applying to both Part B and Part C.

Presented to the Troy School District Board of Education on December 9, 2025.

Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) resolutions packet, five pages, prepared for the association's January 2026 resolution process and circulated to member boards including Troy School District. The header cites OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5, Resolution Adoption: resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts shall be the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors. The packet contains two proposed new resolutions followed by the full set of continuing resolutions previously adopted by the membership, each carrying its adoption and amendment dates.

PROPOSED NEW RESOLUTION #1: OCSBA supports non-partisan school board elections. The stated rationale is that the proposal responds to House Bill 4588, then moving through the state House, with the bill link given as https://legislature.mi.gov/Bills/Bill?ObjectName=2025-HB-4588. The packet argues that partisan school board elections will decrease the number of willing candidates; increase campaign costs, because school board members would have to be successful in two elections, a primary election as well as the November election; align local education decisions with party interests rather than student needs; and exclude thousands of current or potential board members, including federal employees, who are legally prohibited from running in partisan races.

PROPOSED NEW RESOLUTION #2: OCSBA supports full funding of Early On Michigan, an early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays, or who are at risk for delays due to certain health conditions. The rationale states that the resolution is proposed to shine a light on the importance of early intervention programs such as Early On Michigan and on the need for additional state funding to adequately serve families of children already identified as eligible and to serve all children who should be identified as eligible. It explains that the Michigan Mandatory Special Education law (MMSE) requires special education services for eligible children and students from birth through age 25, and that federal law also mandates early intervention programs. Part B of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) refers to special education services for students ages 3 through 21; Part C of IDEA refers to early intervention services for eligible infants and toddlers from birth through age 2, and in Michigan Part C is called Early On; special education supports and services for students age 22 through 25 are part of MMSE. The packet states that OCSBA has always supported early childhood education and that the earlier the intervention begins, the greater the impact. Early On is described as Michigan's statewide, comprehensive, coordinated interagency system of early intervention services for infants and toddlers, birth to age three years, with disabilities and their families; it is coordinated by the Michigan Department of Education and provides services under Part C of IDEA. Local communities receive funding through their local Intermediate School District (ISD) to implement Early On. Each local ISD jurisdiction has an interagency coordinating council, comprised of individuals from human service agencies, parents, educators and other agency personnel who serve families, that guides implementation locally, and implementation is also guided through local memoranda of understanding between education, mental health, public health and social services.

The funding argument states that for 50 years the association has advocated for IDEA funding for students, and that the congressional promise to fund 40% of the cost of providing special education services applies to Part B, children age 3 to 21, and to Part C, early intervention services for infants and toddlers through age 2. Three figures are given for Early On: the estimated annual cost is $230M to provide high-quality early intervention services; the state should appropriate at least $138M, described as 60% of the estimated annual cost; and Section 54d of the FY26 School Aid Act provides state funding of $48M. A reference link is given to the Early On Foundation case for funding document at earlyonfoundation.org.

CONTINUING RESOLUTIONS. ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY (OCSBA adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025): supports holding every school that receives public funding to the same accountability and transparency standards, including FOIA requests and the Open Meetings Act, covering local districts, ISDs, Public School Academies (charter schools), their authorizers and management companies, and all colleges and universities; cites MASB Resolution A 6.65 (c), (d), (f). BROADBAND ACCESS AND DEVICES (adopted 9/11/2021; amended 6/5/2025): broadband should be included in any federal or state infrastructure plan; supports additional federal and state funding to expand affordable and reliable broadband access; supports federal and state programs for the purchase of internet capable devices and software; supports dedicated resources for cybersecurity; cites MASB Resolution A-10.30, 2021 amendment. EARLY CHILDHOOD (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025): supports additional new dollars to fund universal, public preschool for all four year old children, and mandatory kindergarten for all five-year-old children; cites MASB Resolution A 6.15 (c). EVIDENCE-BASED DECISION MAKING (adopted 9/24/2019): supports evidence-based education policy that will maximize opportunities for the highest achievement of each student; cites MASB Resolution G 11.01. LAME DUCK (adopted 9/24/2019): supports lame duck parameters addressing introduction and accelerated passage of legislation after the November election. LOCAL CONTROL (adopted 9/24/2019): supports local control of community-governed public schools with elected school boards; cites MASB Resolutions A 10.10, A 10.55, A 12.70. MENTAL HEALTH (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025): supports increased mental health services and professionals in schools and, at a minimum, annual inflation adjusted state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe; help staff identify potential mental health issues for students; encourage MDE to develop a model policy for staff regarding identifying mental health issues and appropriate staff response; cites MASB Resolutions G 9.01, G 9.05, G 9.50.

SCHOOL AID (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025), four parts: (A) specify that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th grade public education in Michigan's Constitution and oppose any attempts to create private school vouchers or tax credit programs, citing MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (a) and A 10.05; (B) support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students, citing MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (g) and (j) and A 10.55; (C) protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes, citing MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (c) and A 10.55; (D) support enacting the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1 so districts have factual information to meet their constitutional and statutory requirement to approve a budget by June 30, citing MASB Resolution A 10.25 (h). SCHOOL FINANCE RESEARCH COLLABORATIVE (SFRC) (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 9/11/2021, 3/3/2023, 6/5/2025): supports implementation of the SFRC recommendations while holding higher funded districts harmless; cites MASB resolution G 11.01 and A-10.25, 2021 amendment. SCHOOL NUTRITION (adopted 3/3/2023; amended 6/5/2025): supports codification of free universal meals. SCHOOL SAFETY (adopted 3/3/2023): supports adequate state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe. SPECIAL EDUCATION (adopted 9/24/2019): supports full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, noting that although federal legislation initially promised to provide 40 percent of the excess cost to educate students with disabilities, appropriations have fallen short, leaving states and local districts to make up the difference; cites MASB Resolution A 5.01 and NSBA Advocacy: IDEA. TEACHER SHORTAGES (adopted 9/11/2021; amended 6/5/2025): supports statewide initiatives to address teacher shortages and retain teachers while maintaining quality teacher preparation programs, including incentives to enter and complete a teaching college program, incentives for teachers to remain in the classroom, and easing the process to obtain Michigan certification for teachers certified in other states; cites MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority. UNFUNDED MANDATES (adopted 9/24/2019): opposes any state or federal legislation that results in increased costs for school districts without full funding, and encourages the Michigan Legislature to oppose federal laws or programs that are not fully funded and thus cost the state valuable resources; cites MASB Resolution A 10.20.

The packet closes with a statement that, when aligned with OCSBA legislative priorities, OCSBA also supports the National School Boards Association (NSBA) Legislative Agenda, the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Legislative Agenda, the Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) Legislative Agenda, and the Consortium of State School Board Associations (COSSBA) Legislative Agenda (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025), with links to MASB Resolutions at masb.org/resolutions.aspx, NSBA Advocacy at nsba.org/Advocacy, and COSSBA Advocacy at cossba.org/advocacy.

2025_335_ap_spanish_french.paragraph: Presentation slide deck on AP Spanish and AP French resource adoption, prepared for the 12/9/25 Board Workshop and carried to the December 16, 2025 Troy School District Board meeting. Troy's current AP world language texts, Abriendo Paso (2014) for Spanish and T'es Branche (2014) for French, are described as outdated and lacking interpersonal speaking practice and AP test preparation, and the resources adopted in 2017 do not represent current culture. After a selection process guided by Oakland Schools consultant Jen Howe, Vista Higher Learning is recommended over Wayside and Klett, with seven-year licenses beginning in August.
2025_335_ap_spanish_french.page:
**Title:** AP Spanish and AP French Resource Adoption, 12/9/25 Board Workshop, Troy School District.

**Context and rationale.** World Language levels run Level 1 through Level 5 AP; the AP exams are written at the intermediate high / advanced levels. The TSD World Languages vision states that learners can communicate in an ever-expanding global community, experience the heritage of another culture, become resilient risk-takers, improve memory and problem-solving skills, enhance college applications and professional marketability, and open themselves to world travel. AP World Language and Culture is equivalent to an intermediate level college course, with students applying interpersonal, interpretive and presentational modes of communication across themes of family and communities, personal and public identities, beauty and aesthetics, science and technology, contemporary life, and global challenges. The exam assesses both language and culture, but the resources adopted in 2017 do not have current culture represented.

**Current state.** World Languages operates on a 7 year adoption cycle. With the PLC structure, Troy AP World Language teachers desire a common resource to build cohesion among programs. Current resources: Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish, with outdated readings, no interpersonal speaking practice and no AP test prep; T'es Branche (2014) for AP French, a Level 4 textbook with outdated readings and listening resources. Teachers are pulling resources from a wide variety of sources, some at their own cost.

**Selection process.** Facilitated with Jen Howe, Oakland Schools Heritage and World Language Consultant. AP resources timeline: 24-25 school year, exploration of resources; 8/11 leadership planning; 8/20 department kickoff and visioning; 10/2 and 10/7 rubric creation and vendor presentations; 10/20 pilot planning; 11/11 and 11/18 PLC check-ins; 12/2 pilot feedback and synthesis.

**Vendors considered**

| Vendor | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| Wayside | French and Spanish: relatable content with a variety of authentic resources, but does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment and is only a textbook without assessment practice |
| Klett | French: no AP resource. Spanish: many authentic resources and AP practice, but does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment, has fewer resources than Vista, and less user-friendly technology |
| Vista Higher Learning | French and Spanish: matches the rigor of the AP exam, culturally relevant resources and a large resource bank; because of its rigor resources may need scaffolding at the start of the year |

**Vista specifics.** The authors of Vista are also College Board trainers, and Vista has 80% of the AP World Languages market share. The 26-27 AP Exam will be updated, and Vista has agreed to provide an updated crosswalk for launching the 26-27 school year; when it updates its textbooks it will provide updated electronic and physical resources free of cost, and the district will bank its professional learning credit to support the change in August.

**Features shown.** AP French culturally relevant resources, with and without student supports; AP Spanish cultural comparison, in which students compare the country they are studying with the United States, illustrated by Maya sharing how the role of grandparents differs in the United States versus El Salvador; AP Spanish simulated conversations; and an example of interpersonal communication supporting the Free Response AP tasks, which are 50% of the exam.

**Stakeholder support.** Student quotations praise the online textbook for more listening and speaking resources, faster navigation, and portability on an iPad, and credit the ebook with building confidence for the heavily weighted speaking sections of the AP test. Student Survey and Caretaker Survey slides follow, along with a Financial Request slide whose amounts are not captured in the extracted text.

**Timeline moving forward.** December: order placed. January: physical materials inventoried; pilot licenses extended into June. August: 7 year licenses begin and are rostered; PD from Vista with College Board changes.

Slide presentation titled AP Spanish and AP French Resource Adoption, delivered at the 12/9/25 Board Workshop of the Troy School District and appearing on the December 16, 2025 Board of Education agenda. The deck moves through context and rationale, current state, the process of resource selection, vendor comparison, features of the recommended texts, additional stakeholder support, a financial request, and an anticipated timeline.

CONTEXT AND RATIONALE. The World Language sequence is presented as Level 1, Level 2, Level 3, Level 4 and Level 5 AP, with the note that the AP exams are written at the intermediate high and advanced levels. The TSD World Languages vision statement holds that World Language learners can communicate in an ever-expanding global community; discover and experience the rich heritage of another culture; become resilient risk-takers with a greater capacity to adapt to new environments; improve their memory and problem-solving skills for better overall academic performance; enhance their college applications and increase their professional marketability; and open themselves up to opportunities for world travel. The AP overview states that AP World Language and Culture is equivalent to an intermediate level college course, in which students cultivate their understanding of language and culture by applying interpersonal, interpretive and presentational modes of communication in real life situations while exploring concepts related to family and communities, personal and public identities, beauty and aesthetics, science and technology, contemporary life, and global challenges. The deck notes that the exam assesses both language and culture, but that the resources adopted in 2017 do not have current culture represented.

CURRENT STATE. World Languages follows a 7 year adoption cycle. With the PLC structure in place, Troy AP World Language teachers desire a common resource to help build cohesion among programs. The current resources are Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish, described as having outdated readings that have not been updated, no interpersonal speaking practice and no AP test prep; and T'es Branche (2014) for AP French, described as a Level 4 textbook with outdated readings and listening resources that have not been updated. The current reality slide states that teachers are doing their best to pull resources from a wide variety of sources, some even at their own costs.

PROCESS OF RESOURCE SELECTION. The process was supported by Jen Howe, Oakland Schools Heritage and World Language Consultant. The AP resources timeline lists: the 24-25 school year for exploration of resources; 8/11 leadership planning; 8/20 department kickoff and visioning; 10/2 and 10/7 rubric creation and vendor presentations; 10/20 pilot planning; 11/11 and 11/18 PLC planning and check-ins; and 12/2 pilot feedback and synthesis.

AP VENDORS CONSIDERED, PROS AND CONS. Wayside, for French and Spanish: while the resource has relatable content for students with a variety of authentic resources, it does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment, and it is only a textbook without assessment practice. Klett, for French: no AP resource. Klett, for Spanish: while the resource has a lot of authentic resources and AP practice, it does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment, it does not have the number of resources that Vista has, and the technology was less user friendly. Vista Higher Learning, for French and Spanish: the resource matches the rigor of the AP exam and provides meaningful resources that are culturally relevant as well as a large resource bank, and because of its rigor resources may need to be scaffolded at the start of the year. Additional Vista points: the authors of Vista are also College Board trainers; Vista has 80% of the AP World Languages market share; the 26-27 AP Exam will be updated and Vista has agreed to provide an updated crosswalk for launching the 26-27 school year; when Vista updates its textbooks it will provide the district updated electronic and physical resources free of cost; and the district will bank its professional learning credit to support this change in August.

FEATURES OF RECOMMENDED TEXTS. Sample slides cover AP French culturally relevant resources and AP French culturally relevant resources with student supports. An AP Spanish cultural comparison slide explains that on the AP test students must compare the country they are studying with the United States, illustrated by a segment in which Maya shares how the role of grandparents is different in the United States versus El Salvador. A further slide shows AP Spanish simulated conversations, described as a free response task on the AP exam, and another gives an example of interpersonal communication that fosters student confidence and practice for the Free Response AP tasks, which the deck states are 50% of the exam.

ADDITIONAL STAKEHOLDER SUPPORT. Two student comments are quoted. The first: the student likes an online textbook because it has more resources such as listening and speaking, allows better and faster navigation of pages, and makes it easier to have the textbook on an iPad. The second: the student has used the ebook many times in class and found the variety of resources really helpful, notes that the hardest part of learning Spanish at this high a level is being able to speak their thoughts about everything, and reports that the ebook provided speaking practice that has already increased confidence in speaking ability, adding that the speaking sections of the AP test are huge, very important for the overall score, and heavily weighted, so having these resources builds confidence in trying to earn a good score. The deck then includes a Student Survey slide and a Caretaker Survey slide, whose underlying results are not captured in the extracted text.

FINANCIAL REQUEST AND TIMELINE. A Financial Request section appears in the deck; no dollar figures for the request are present in the extracted text. The anticipated timeline moving forward is given in three columns: December, order placed; January, physical materials inventoried and pilot licenses extended into June; August, 7 year licenses begin and are rostered, with professional development from Vista covering the College Board changes. The deck ends with a Questions slide.
